bibliography.abstract: Bundles and mobility-as-a-service (MaaS) plans are seen as promising instruments to integrate shared electric micromobility with public transit, yet evidence on effective designs and their real-world uptake remains scarce. In a first step, we use a stated choice experiment among Swiss residents (n = 1, 422 across two samples) and estimate mixed logit models to assess preferences for three subscription bundle types (flat rates, 50% discount passes, minute packages) and single-journey bundles. In a second step, we compare the model-implied market shares with sales data from a 10-week pilot in Eastern Switzerland. Prior experience of shared micromobility services emerged as the dominant predictor of bundle utility. We document a substantial gap between stated preference and adoption: only 2.4-4.6% of hypothetical interest translates into purchases. Despite this gap, the sales compare favorably to previous MaaS trials. The results imply that practitioners should anticipate considerably lower uptake than is indicated by survey-based projections.

en.caveats: The real-world sales data is derived from a relatively short 10-week pilot program in a single region of Switzerland, which may not fully capture long-term adoption dynamics.
en.what: This study evaluated preferences for public transit and shared micromobility subscription bundles using a stated choice experiment with 1,422 Swiss residents, comparing the model-implied market shares against actual sales data from a 10-week pilot in Eastern Switzerland. The analysis revealed that prior experience with shared micromobility is the strongest predictor of bundle utility, and identified a massive gap between hypothetical interest and real-world adoption, with only 2.4% to 4.6% of stated preferences translating into actual purchases.
en.why: It quantifies a severe overestimation bias in survey-based projections for Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) uptake, providing a concrete calibration metric for planners and operators who previously relied on stated-preference data to design and fund integrated mobility schemes.
